newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban fight in conquered city, cross key pass.
newsitem.headline: Taleban fight in conquered city, cross key pass.

text.p: Shi'ite Moslem residents fought the Taleban militia in this newly conquered northern Afghan city on Tuesday while Teleban forces said they had pushed through a key pass into opposition territory north of Kabul.
Heavy fighting erupted in many parts of Mazar-i-Sharif after armed Shi'ite residents killed three looters they said to belong to the purist Islamic Taleban militia, witnesses said.
Machine gun fire rattled through the streets amid the crash of rocket-propelled grenades as Taleban fighters battled the Shi'ites in the city's northern district of Saidabad.
"All the people started fighting the Taleban because they were taking television sets and everything from people's homes, even children's toys," said Sadiqullah, a Shi'ite resident.
"They are not human. If they were human we would join them, but they are wild men," he said, quivering with rage..

It was not immediately clear whether the ethnic Uzbek followers of General Abdul Malik, who changed sides last week and handed most of northern Afghanistan to the Taleban, had joined the fighting. Malik's men are supposed to be operating as a joint security force with the Taleban.

The fighting started late in the afternoon and The Taleban and Malik's men are supposed to be operating as a joint security force in the north, but it was not immediately clear if both groups were in action against the Shi'ites.
"All the people started fighting the Taleban because they were taking television sets and everything from people's homes, even children's toys," said Sadiqullah, a Shi'ite resident.
"They are not human. If they were human we would join them, but they are wild men," he said, quivering with anger.
The fighting started late in the afternoon and tracer bullets were still streaking the sky after dark.

The Taleban government in Kabul, which now controls at least nine-tenths of the country, said in a radio broadcast its forces had crossed the strategic 11,000-foot (3,350-metre) high Salang Pass on Tuesday and taken the district of Khenjan in Baghlan province.

The advance, after two days of fighting, will cut the last link between Hezb-i-Wahadat, a mainly Shi'ite faction still fighting theTaleban in the central province of Bamiyan, and Ahmed Shah Masood, military commander of the government driven from Kabul last September.
Taleban says that Masood, who is bottled up in the north-east, has contacted Kabul and suggested peace talks.
Taleban supreme leader Mullah Mohammad Omar authorised Defence Minister Mullah Abdullah to talk to Masood, spokesman Mullah Abdul Wakil told the Pakistan-based agency Afghan Islamic Press.
Russia convened a meeting in Moscow on Tuesday with diplomats from the former Soviet states bordering Afghanistan.

Foreign Ministry spokesman Gennady Tarasov told reporters that Moscow saw the Taleban advance as an internal Afghan matter but "if the borders are violated then measures will be taken under the Collective Security Treaty."
